questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What would establish a claim of borrowing
questions.learningObjective: Set out what would establish a claim of borrowing.
questions.stem: A revision card asks what would count as proof that one writer borrowed from another.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that proof in this area is cumulative rather than a single piece. The group needs the earlier text to have existed and to have been available, needs the later text to have drawn on it in ways that go beyond coincidence, and needs the common-source explanation ruled out so that the resemblance cannot be accounted for in some other way. Each of these can fail independently, and an argument that skips one of them will be answered by the simplest objection: that both writers used the same material.

questions.explanation: Proof here is cumulative, and each condition can fail on its own: availability, use beyond coincidence, and excluding a common source. An argument that skips one will meet the objection that both used the same material.
questions.hint: Ask which condition of proof the group has skipped.

questions.explanation: An influence argument is a sequence in which each stage rules out an alternative explanation, and the decisive stage excludes a common source. Listing the stages or stopping early leaves the work undone.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that the difference between two treatments of one fact is best measured by what each text does with it: what is asserted, what is left unsaid, who is allowed to know it, and what the reader is asked to conclude. answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that grading evidence by the claim it can carry protects an argument from being overstated. questions.stem: An earlier edition has a chapter that the later edition replaces, and the group builds an argument from it.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that an argument about influence runs through steps, and each step has to be evidenced in order. The group must first show that the earlier text existed and was available, then show that the later writer had access to it, then show that the resemblance is not explainable by a common source, and only then may they say that the later text was shaped by the earlier. questions.explanation: An influence argument needs availability, access, resemblance and the exclusion of common cause, in that order. Skipping a step leaves the conclusion resting on resemblance alone.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that proof in this area is cumulative rather than a single piece. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Evidence graded by the claim it can carry
questions.learningObjective: Explain why evidence is graded by the claim it carries.
questions.stem: A revision sheet asks how strong each piece of evidence is and the group has to write it plainly.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that the strength of evidence is a matter of what it can be asked to prove, and that the group should say so in plain terms rather than reaching for vague words such as strong or convincing. A distinctive shared detail might carry a claim that one writer knew the other's work, a widely shared formula cannot carry that claim, and documentary evidence of access can carry a direct statement about reading. Writing the strength out forces the group to notice when a claim has outgrown its support.

questions.explanation: Strength of evidence is a matter of what it can be asked to prove, and the group should say that plainly rather than reaching for vague words. Writing it out also exposes any claim that has outgrown its support.
questions.hint: Ask what each piece can be asked to prove.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Evidential steps of an influence argument
questions.learningObjective: Order the evidential steps of an influence argument.
questions.stem: The group tries to state the steps of an influence argument and finds one step keeps getting skipped.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that the step usually skipped is the exclusion of a common source, and that without it the argument never rises above a resemblance. The group should set out the steps explicitly: show that the earlier text existed, show it was available to the later writer, show that the later text uses it in ways that go beyond coincidence, and then rule out a third text or account that both writers might have shared. Only the third of these is usually skipped, and it is the one the objector will reach for.

questions.explanation: The common-source step turns a resemblance into a claim about influence, and skipping it leaves the argument open to the simplest objection. Adding quotations repeats a step rather than supplying it.
questions.hint: Ask which step the argument keeps omitting.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A difference offered in page layout
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a difference in page layout can demonstrate.
questions.stem: A revision exercise asks what the group can claim from a difference in how two books set out their lists.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that a difference in layout demonstrates something about how a text organises attention, since the reader's eye and the pace of reading follow the arrangement. It can therefore support a claim about emphasis, about the relation between an aside and the main text, or about how the book wants to be handled, provided the group says which of those it is claiming. What it cannot demonstrate is that one text copied another, since printing conventions travel and are shared.

questions.explanation: A layout difference shows how a text organises attention, so it supports claims about emphasis and about an aside's relation to the main text. It cannot demonstrate copying, since conventions travel between books.
questions.hint: Ask what layout shows about the organisation of attention.
